newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cattle herd shrinking but tide seen turning.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cattle herd shrinking but tide seen turning.

text.p: A further reduction in the supply of cattle and calves will be indicated when the U.S. Department of Agriculture issues its semi-annual Cattle Inventory report on Friday, livestock analysts said.
But there have been signs during the last month or two that the tide is already starting to turn, they added.

"We are certainly through the bulk of the liquidation phase of the cattle cycle. Next year on July 1 we may not be any higher but we probably won't be any lower," said analyst Jim Robb of the Livestock Marketing Information Center.

A Reuter survey of analysts produced an average estimate for the total number of U.S. cattle and calves, as of July 1, of 109.11 million head, down from 112.00 million a year earlier and 113.00 million as of July 1, 1995.
"It takes several years for the cattle market to turn the corner and be clearly in an uptrend but we're probably at the bottom of the curve at this point," Robb said.
He noted that calf-cow operations were now making money.
"Compared to last year at this time, this market is night and day different and this will be reflected a year from now," Robb said.
Tom Morgan, president of Morgan Research Group, also said a turning point in the cattle cycle had been reached.

"We are in the transition part of the cattle cycle. The report is probably going to show continued liquidation of the beef cow herd and we've seen some decline in the dairy cow herd but this will be the low point because we're about to switch gears," Morgan said.
The Reuter analysts' survey produced an average estimate for the calf crop of 38.54 million head, down from 39.80 million a year earlier, a decline of 3.2 percent.
"Not only was the calf crop smaller than the previous year we also imported slightly fewer cattle the first half of the year," said analyst Chuck Levitt of Alaron Trading Corp.
He noted there was a lot of talk about death loss in calves during the winter storms in the northern Prairie states.
"The death loss figure that I used was similar to a year ago but a year ago we had a much larger herd so the death loss as a proportion to the total herd was bigger this year," Levitt said.
The Cattle Inventory Report is due to be released on Friday at 1400 CDT/1900 GMT.
